To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain drain is an important phenomenon that affects the global distribution of knowledge and skills, that it is a problem for the sending countries, and that it has a positive effect on the receiving countries, but that the positive effects of the brain drain on the sending countries are much smaller than the negative effects.

(1) the brain drain from developing countries has a positive effect on their income growth; (2) this effect is stronger for countries with a lower initial income; (3) the effect is stronger in countries with a higher share of skilled migrants in the total population; (4) this effect is driven by the positive effect of the brain gain on total factor productivity; (5) the positive effect on total factor productivity is stronger for countries that have a higher share of highly educated migrants; and

1. the brain drain has negative impacts on the home countries of migrants, but the size of the impact depends on the skill level of the migrants, 2. the negative impacts are larger for the countries that lose the most skilled workers and 3. the negative impacts of the brain drain are larger for developing countries than for developed countries.
